items.title: Beethoven - Egmont Overture, Op. 84 (Czech National Symphony Orchestra, Musopen Kickstarter recording)
items.creator: Ludwig van Beethoven (composer, d. 1827); Czech National Symphony Orchestra for Musopen (performers)
items.date: Composed 1809-1810; recorded in Prague c. 2011-2012 for the Musopen Kickstarter project; archive.org upload 2012-08-08
items.use_for: FIRST CHOICE. The coda section 440.0-458.0 fits the arc almost exactly: hushed woodwind chords, then a 1 s silence, then a pp-to-fff string crescendo (renaissance sketch -> blueprint -> Mars -> radiation -> suit/habitat) that arrives on the triumphant F-major 'Victory' tutti at 455.3-456.5, where MARSOPS lands. Serious that turns to triumphant; classy; no lyrics.
items.depicts: Full symphony orchestra; serious F-minor drama that resolves into a triumphant F-major coda with brass and timpani

items.measurements: File 540.94 s, MP3 48 kHz stereo ~323 kb/s. Whole-track integrated -15.0 LUFS, LRA 18.7 LU, true peak -0.8 dBFS. BEST 15-18 s: 440.0-458.0 (-14.2 LUFS, peak -0.9 dBFS): quiet woodwind chords at about -25 dB (relative to the loudest second) up to 442.0; near-silence at 442.25-443.0 (-55 dB); string crescendo from 443.25 (-24 dB) rising without a break (450 s -16, 453 s -8, 455.25 s -3); fff arrival at 456.0-456.5 (-1 dB; 456 s is the loudest second of the whole overture) with a second accent at 457.75. Just before it, at 421.75-425.0, are the dramatic tutti chords and then the 427.5-429.0 silence (you can start at 421.0 for a two-part 'strike - hush - build' version). REAL ENDING: repeated F-major tutti chords at 526.0, 527.5, 529.25, 532.25, 534.0, 535.5, 537.25, 538.0 and the final chord at 539.0; sound gone by 539.75 (file ends 540.94); last 15.9 s (525.0-540.9) -12.2 LUFS, LRA 2.2. OPENING: sostenuto chords hit at 1.0, 6.0 and 12.0 s. Tempo: orchestral rubato, no steady beat (autocorrelation strength 0.09).

items.use_for: The darkest, most urgent option, good for the radiation threat: 676.0-694.0 is a steady 18 s orchestral build to a brass climax at 693.0-693.25. Alternative 720.0-738.5 builds to the movement's loudest moment at 738.25. For a silence-then-shock cut, the famous fff explosion after the pppp passage is at 540.25.

items.creator: Ludwig van Beethoven (composer, d. 1827); Czech National Symphony Orchestra for Musopen (performers)
items.date: Composed 1807; recorded c. 2011-2012 for the Musopen Kickstarter project; archive.org upload 2012-08-08
items.use_for: Built-in punctuation for a three-act cut. The opening 0.0-16.5 is three statements of a held unison string note followed by a hammer-blow tutti chord and a silence. Use the chords at 3.5 / 9.5 / 15.5 for renaissance -> blueprint -> Mars, and fill the silences with the drawing SFX. It is not a crescendo build, so pair it with a title card on the third chord, or extend to 20.0 for two more chords (18.0, 19.5).
items.depicts: Full orchestra; stern C-minor unison notes and short fortissimo chords separated by dramatic silences

items.use_for: The best 'button' ending in the set: a hushed fade and then two huge final chords, 2.0 s apart (765.25 = MARSOPS, 767.25 = 'Coming soon'). Use it as the last 4.5 s (765.0-769.75) after another track's build, or alone as 752.0-769.75. The quiet 752-765 part sits 30-50 dB under the chords, so it needs about 15-20 dB of gain or compression to carry visuals.

items.title: Richard Strauss - Feierlicher Einzug der Ritter des Johanniter-Ordens (US Marine Band, album 'Music of Richard Strauss')
items.creator: Richard Strauss (composer, d. 1949); 'The President's Own' United States Marine Band (performers)
items.date: Composed 1909; recorded 1996 (archive.org metadata date 1996-05; the ID3 tag says 2001)
items.use_for: Ceremonial brass and timpani (a knightly procession), majestic and classy. 78.0-96.0 is a slow, even brass crescendo that peaks on a plateau (94.0-95.5) rather than a sharp hit. 391.0-407.5 is the full-brass ending with a long held final chord (401.25-406.0) and a clean cutoff, which works well under the end card. Lower priority: see the rights note.
items.depicts: Brass choir (trumpets, horns, trombones, tubas) with timpani; fanfare-like processional
items.evidence: Recording: performed by the US Marine Band, a US federal government ensemble, so it is a US government work (17 U.S.C. 105). archive.org item 'MusicOfRichardStrauss' (creator United States Marine Band) carries the Public Domain Mark 1.0. Its description says: 'All these compositions and their arrangements if any are public domain in the United States as published before 1923.' It also says the album's Rosenkavalier suite and Festmusik der Stadt Wien were left out for rights reasons. The official Marine Band album page (marineband.marines.mil/Audio-Resources/Marine-Band-Albums/Music-of-Richard-Strauss/, Album No. 16, recorded 1996) confirms the album and track 7, but it returned HTTP 403 here, so the booklet's arranger credit could NOT be read. The work is written for brass and timpani (published descriptions list 15 trumpets, 4 horns, 4 trombones, 2 tubas, timpani), so most likely no arrangement is involved. Composition: published 1909, so public domain in the US; Strauss died 1949, so public domain in life+70 countries (EU, UK) since 1 Jan 2020. A few longer-term countries (e.g. Spain, life+80 for authors who died before 1987) protect it until the end of 2029.

rejected_or_unavailable.what: Holst 'Mars, the Bringer of War' - US Air Force Heritage of America Band (Wikimedia Commons File:Holst-_mars.ogg; same recording as the OpenGameArt 'Holst - The Planets (Public Domain).zip' marked CC0)
rejected_or_unavailable.why: The recording is a US government work, but the Commons page credits 'Merlin Patterson's transcription, edited by Capt. Lang and MSgt Aldo Forte' (CD 'Frontiers', 1998). Patterson's wind-band transcription is a modern copyrighted arrangement (derivative work), so using it in an ad would need the arranger's permission. Rejected. Other wind-band versions found (Reed/McAlister) are also modern copyrighted arrangements. Public-domain orchestral Mars recordings are only historic 1920s discs: Holst's 1926 electrical recording stays under US copyright until at least 1 Jan 2027, and the 1922-23 acoustic one is too low-fidelity for an ad.
Offline: the homepage now says the service has been taken down.
The archive.org zip member returned HTTP 503 twice; not needed.
